opus-5.5.text:
That's a hard question, because "greatest" can mean very different things. One way is to ask which work changed the most people's research, which had the biggest downstream impact. Another is to ask which work was most surprising, most against the consensus at the time it came out. Those two don't always line up.

If I had to pick one, I'd probably lean toward something like the Transformer, "Attention Is All You Need." Not because the idea was the most elegant in some abstract sense, but because it became a kind of universal substrate. Almost everything that happened afterward, GPT, BERT, scaling laws, multimodal models, agents, sits on top of it. A great work, to me, isn't only a clever trick. It's something that becomes infrastructure, so that later people don't even think of it as a contribution anymore. It just becomes the default.

But I also think there's a deeper way to look at it. Many of the most important works in AI aren't really about a method. They're about redefining the problem. GPT-3 is a good example. Architecturally it wasn't that new, but it showed that a single model, through prompting, could do many tasks. That changed how people thought about what a "task" even is. In some sense, the greatest works change the question that everyone is working on, not just the answer.

That's also how I think about my own field. In the first half of AI, the focus was on building better methods and climbing benchmarks. Now we have a recipe that works pretty generally, so the bottleneck shifts to what problems we define and how we evaluate them. So if you ask what makes a work great going forward, I think it's more and more about defining the right problem, finding the right environment, the right evaluation, the thing that really matters for utility in the real world.

So my short answer is: the Transformer if you're looking for impact, but the deeper criterion is whether a work changes what the whole community thinks is worth doing.

r001.rationale: The response describes later AI developments as building on the Transformer, which became shared infrastructure and a default foundation. This clearly presents progress as cumulative.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the question itself reveals something about how people usually think about AI, which is in terms of individual works—a paper, a model, a benchmark. But if I'm being candid, I don't think there is a single greatest work, and I'm a little suspicious of the framing.

When I look back at what actually moved the field, it's rarely one paper. Take the Transformer—everyone points to "Attention Is All You Need" as the obvious answer. But that paper mattered because of what came after it: scaling laws, GPT, the realization that you could just keep going. The Transformer paper alone, in 2017, was a better machine translation architecture. It became "the greatest work" retroactively, because a lot of other people did a lot of other things on top of it.

So if you force me to choose, I'd say the greatest work isn't a paper, it's an idea that kept being right over and over: that you can take a general-purpose learning method, give it more data and more compute, and it keeps getting better. Sutton's "Bitter Lesson" articulates it, but even that is more of an observation than a work. The idea predates the essay.

The second thing I'd say is that I think about this in terms of paradigm shifts rather than contributions. A paper that improves a benchmark by five points is a contribution. A paper that changes what questions people ask is a paradigm shift. By that standard, I'd actually put things like the original deep RL work on Atari, or GPT-3's in-context learning result, higher than works that were technically more sophisticated, because they changed what people believed was possible.

And personally—maybe this is biased because of my own work on agents—I think the transition we're in right now, where language models stop being things that produce text and start being things that take actions in environments, is going to look in hindsight like one of these moments. But it's hard to point at a single work for it. It's a shift that's happening across many papers and many groups at once.

So my honest answer is: I'd resist picking one. Not out of modesty, but because I think the "single greatest work" lens actually makes you worse at predicting what will matter next. The things that matter are usually only obvious several years later, and they tend to be ideas rather than artifacts.

r001.rationale: The response says the Transformer paper mattered because later work built on it, and that field-changing advances often emerge from many papers and groups over time.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s hard to choose one without first asking what we mean by “greatest.” Is it the work that introduced the most important idea, the work that made something useful possible, or the work that changed how people think about intelligence? Those might lead to different answers.

AI is also cumulative. A breakthrough depends on earlier ideas, on systems, and on people figuring out how to make those ideas work. Picking one paper can hide that history.

So I’d rather ask which work changed the questions we’re able to ask. For me, that’s a useful way to think about greatness: not just whether a work solved a problem, but whether it opened up a new direction.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly describes AI as cumulative and says breakthroughs depend on earlier ideas, systems, and implementation work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s hard to choose just one, because “greatest” can mean different things. Do you mean the most original idea, the work that influenced the most researchers, or the system that changed how people use AI? Those might lead to very different answers.

There’s also a question of timing. A piece of work can look modest when it comes out, but become foundational ten years later. And something that feels revolutionary today might turn out to be one step in a much longer process. So I’d be more interested in discussing what makes a work great than trying to name a single winner.

r001.rationale: The response says a work may become foundational over time and that a breakthrough may be one step in a longer process, but it does not communicate that AI advances build on earlier work.
